take_homes: Keep the judge fixed and let only the tactic file change. That is the only reason the score means anything.
A flat score tells me about the judge, not the work. I have to score a handful by hand against it, and I should have a judge for 'makes the reader act' as well as one for 'grounded'.
Decide in advance what the agent may send without me (draft, review first, send to myself, automatic). Keep reading one real output myself.

monday.move: Run the groundedness judge on the usage-pricing pilot brief with fresh data. Score five outputs by hand and compare with the judge. Draft a steering judge for the pricing working group's mails.
monday.who: Me first, then one person from my team to review the judge
monday.when: Monday morning for the hand-scoring, the loop on Tuesday
monday.stop_condition: If the judge passes things I'd send back, I fix the judge before running any loop. If three rounds don't improve the score, I stop and read the outputs myself.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context files and the judge, so everyone keeps their own copy. The loop is only useful if the judge and tactic live in one place.

misconception.why: I still believe prompts matter. But here the improvement comes from a fixed judge and a rewritten tactic file, so the gain is in the loop and the yardstick, not in a cleverer prompt. It is not fully changed, since the tactic is a kind of prompt.

one_line: Good middle: the fixed-judge idea and 'check the judge too' are worth the hour, but the recap slides and the repeated yardstick line could be cut.
